draft.title: Causes of crime
card: No single cause explains crime. Several factors can combine, and each one can contribute to a person offending without forcing them to.
Social and economic
factors such as poverty, unemployment and disadvantage. They can limit a person's access to money, education or support, which can make offending more likely.
Psychological
factors that affect how a person thinks or behaves, such as poor impulse control or a mental illness. They can contribute to some offences.
Opportunity and peers
a chance to offend, such as an unlocked car, can contribute to crime. So can pressure from friends or a group to join in.
draft.remember: Crime can have many causes, and they often work together.

a.q: Which statement best shows that crime can have more than one cause?
opts: Poverty and peer pressure can both contribute to offending
Poverty is the only factor that leads people to offend
Peer pressure always makes a person commit a crime
Opportunity decides whether any person offends or not
a.why: The card says several factors can combine and each one can contribute. The other options treat one factor as the only cause or say it always forces offending, which the card does not support.
a.clue: Look for the option that allows more than one factor and does not say always or only.

b.q: Jaden, 16, has no job. One night his friends dare him to take a bike left unlocked outside a shop, and he does. Which pair of factors is most clearly shown?
b.why: His friends dared him, which is peer pressure, and the bike was unlocked, which gave him the opportunity. The story says nothing about a mental illness or impulse control. His lack of a job is mentioned, but it is not the pair the scenario shows most clearly.
b.clue: Find what his friends did and what the shop left out.

a.best: Poverty and peer pressure can both contribute to offending

problems.detail: The clue gives the answer away. It tells students to pick the option that allows more than one factor and avoids 'always' or 'only', so they can answer without knowing the idea.

The right option is the only hedged one ('can both contribute'). Every distractor uses an absolute word ('decides', 'always', 'only'), so the right option stands out without any knowledge of the causes of crime.
The clue says 'what the shop left out', but the scenario says the bike was left unlocked outside a shop, not by the shop. The clue is inaccurate and also points almost directly at the answer.

check.summary: The card and answers are accurate. Question a's clue and its only-hedged right option give the answer away, and question b's clue wrongly says the shop left the bike out and nearly hands over the answer.

a.q: Lena grew up in poverty and left school early with few chances of work. What type of factor do these details show?
a.why: Poverty and leaving school early limit Lena's access to money and education, so they are social and economic factors. Psychological factors are about how a person thinks or behaves, such as impulse control, and nothing in the details describes that.
a.clue: Are these details about Lena's mind or her circumstances?

b.q: Jaden, 16, is walking home with friends. They dare him to take a bike left unlocked outside a shop, and he does. Which two factors does the story show?
b.why: His friends dared him, which is peer pressure, and the unlocked bike gave him the chance to offend, which is opportunity. Each other option pairs one of these with a factor the story never mentions, such as poverty, unemployment or a mental illness.
b.clue: Count only the factors the story actually describes.
